title: Diwali: the row of lamps
hook: Rama comes home after fourteen years, and a whole city lights lamps to show him the way

segments.voice: Yesterday: Navaratri's tenth day, Ravana burned, Durga sent home, first letters in rice. Nine nights, then the dawn.

The day after Diwali's Lakshmi night has a guest of its own. In Maharashtra and Karnataka, families light lamps and welcome back a king. Not Rama: a king the gods defeated. In Maharashtra, some say a line that goes, roughly: let troubles go, and let Bali's kingdom come. Bali was a demon king, an asura. So why would anyone light lamps for the return of a demon? Because of how he lost.
screen: `THE DAY AFTER THE LAKSHMI NIGHT.` → `A KING COMES BACK.` → `A DEMON KING.`

segments.voice: The Bhagavata Purana tells it in its eighth book. Bali, grandson of Prahlad, the boy from the Holi fire, has become so powerful and so generous that he rules all three worlds, and the gods have lost their places. Vishnu comes to restore the balance as Vamana, a small boy, a young brahmin student with an umbrella and a water pot, at a great sacrifice Bali is holding. Bali is known for never refusing a guest. Ask for anything, he says. The boy asks for three steps of land, measured by his own feet. Bali laughs: ask for more. But Bali's teacher, Shukra, sees through it and warns him: this is Vishnu, and he'll take everything. Bali thinks about it, and gives anyway. I promised, he says, and I won't take back my word. Then the boy grows. One step covers the earth, the second the heavens, and there's nowhere left for the third. So Bali bows and offers his own head. Vishnu places his foot there and sends Bali down to a lower realm, Sutala. But the Bhagavata doesn't end it as a punishment. Vishnu praises Bali's truthfulness and promises to stand guard at his door himself. In many tellings, Bali may come back to the earth once a year to visit his people, and in parts of western and southern India that visit is the day after the Lakshmi night, Bali Pratipada. So the lamps have one more job: lighting the way home for a king who kept his word when it cost him everything.
screen: `VAMANA: A BOY ASKS FOR THREE STEPS.` · `SHUKRA WARNS; BALI GIVES ANYWAY.` · `THE THIRD STEP ON BALI'S HEAD.` · `BALI PRATIPADA: HIS YEARLY VISIT.` · then, large: `A KING WHO KEPT HIS WORD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one promise that has grown heavier than you expected: a favor, a visit, a job you said yes to. Don't decide anything yet; just hold it the way Bali held his word, the warning in one ear and the promise in the other. Breathe with both.
Diwali. In parts of India, the day after the Lakshmi night welcomes back King Bali, who gave three steps of land and kept his word.

howItsDone: In Maharashtra, Karnataka and nearby regions, the day after the main Diwali night is kept as Bali Pratipada, honoring King Bali's yearly return; in many places it is also a new-year day and a day of gifts between husbands and wives.

fork.setup: you're King Bali. you've promised a boy three steps of land. your teacher warns you the boy is Vishnu and will take everything. what do you do?
fork.reveal: Bali keeps his word. two steps cover earth and heaven, and he offers his own head for the third.

original.note: Sanskrit vāmana: a dwarf, small one. Vishnu's form as the boy who asks for three steps.

trapdoor: what you thought: in Hindu stories, demons are simply the bad guys.
what it means: Bali, an asura, is honored for generosity and for keeping his word, and welcomed back at Diwali.
what a scholar hears: the Bhagavata Purana's eighth book tells Vamana and Bali; the Diwali-time Bali Pratipada is regional, and Kerala's Onam honors Bali's return in a different season.

chat.says: Why would anyone light lamps to welcome back a demon king?
options: Bali kept his word to Vamana though it cost him everything, so he's honored.
Lighting lamps keeps Bali away, so he can't take back the three worlds.
Bali defeated Vishnu in the story, so people celebrate his victory.
chat.meaning: In the Bhagavata, Bali gives Vamana the three steps despite Shukra's warning; Vishnu praises his truthfulness, and many welcome his yearly visit with lamps.

notes: The Marathi saying ('ida pida javo, Baliche rajya yevo': let troubles go, let Bali's kingdom come) is paraphrased, not quoted; confirm.
Confirm Bhagavata 8.18–23 details: Shukra's warning, Bali's refusal to break his word, the third step on his head, Sutala, and Vishnu guarding his door.
Bali's yearly return: associated with Bali Pratipada in western and southern India and with Onam in Kerala; confirm phrasing.
Bali as grandson of Prahlad: confirm (Bali is son of Virochana, son of Prahlada).
